So there’s no easy way to know exactly what happened here because all I have access to is this tweet:
Capital One announced today they will acquire Brex for $5.15 Billion
CEO & Founder Sam Blond announced his departure effective immediately
pic.twitter.com/FsQ9pNkFJt
— Myles Hatz (@M_Hatz)
February 10, 2026
It looks like it was $5.15 Billion.  That’s what Capital One said.  But Brex itself wasn’t clear.  It just said “terms were agreed” in a release.  We don’t really know yet if it was truly $5 Billion (with some cash), $5.15 Billion, etc.  Or even how much cash vs stock was involved.
What we do know is a few things … First, Brex had raised at $12.3 Billion pre-money valuations (Oct ’22) then fell dramatically during the downturn to < $1 Billion (!).  So whatever deal they got would likely be far lower than its peak valuation.
Second, it doesn’t look like anyone in the public markets thought Brex could get anywhere close to a $12B exit anymore.  Even at ~$600m ARR, getting even a $1B+ exit was probably seen by many as a stretch given current multiples.  The market cap of public companies doing similar things like Ramp, Navan, etc. aren’t trading anywhere near where Brex peaked at a $12B valuation.
Third, Brex isn’t the first startup to see the bar go up during the downturn.  And fourth, it shows how tough times can lead to founder departures.  Not always a bad thing per se, but often not fun for everyone.  A bit more on that
here
.
And a reminder that while VCs want founders who win, they also need them to survive long enough to have something left over for investors.  Sometimes that means letting folks go to focus resources on survival and growth.

A startup raises a bunch of money at a crazy high valuation and then they get bought by a big tech company for … much less than the headline number. When companies like this sell early – whether through acquisition or IPO – founders often frame it as "winning" regardless of the ultimate financial outcome. They'll say they created hundreds of millions in wealth for employees, investors, and themselves. They'll point to their legacy, their impact on the market, their ability to attract top talent. All those points are valid. But the reality is more complicated.
